questions.enonce_markdown:
Aspects of the humanity of Jesus are clearly highlighted in the fourth Gospel. Comment on this statement.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Fourth Gospel is often said to stress the divinity of Jesus, for it begins with the Word who was with God and was God (1:1) and records the "I am" sayings. Yet the same Gospel declares that "the Word became flesh and lived among us" (1:14), and it shows Jesus as fully human in many ways. The statement is therefore correct.

**1. The Word became flesh.** The prologue states the incarnation: the eternal Word truly entered human life (1:14). From the start the Gospel affirms that the divine Son is also a real man.

**2. Physical needs and limits.**
- At Jacob's well Jesus is "tired out by his journey" and sits down by the well, and he asks the Samaritan woman for a drink (4:6-7).
- On the cross he says "I am thirsty" (19:28).
- At the end, a soldier pierces his side and blood and water come out, a sign of a real body that has died (19:34).

**3. Emotions.**
- He weeps at the tomb of Lazarus (11:35) and is "greatly disturbed in spirit and deeply moved" (11:33).
- He says "Now my soul is troubled" as the hour of his death approaches (12:27), and he is "troubled in spirit" when he speaks of the betrayal (13:21).
- He loves Martha, her sister and Lazarus (11:5), and the beloved disciple is spoken of as the one whom Jesus loved (13:23).

**4. Human relationships and conduct.** Jesus attends a wedding at Cana with his mother and disciples (2:1-11), washes his disciples' feet like a servant (13:1-17), and from the cross entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple (19:26-27), which shows the care of a son. He is called a man by his opponents and by Pilate ("Here is the man!", 19:5).

**5. Human dependence on the Father.** Jesus says that the Son can do nothing on his own (5:19) and that he does the will of the one who sent him (4:34). This is expressed as obedience, which is a human way of relating to God.

**6. Purpose.** By stressing the humanity of Jesus, the evangelist shows that salvation was brought through a real life, death and resurrection and not by a mere appearance. It may also answer the idea that Jesus only seemed to be human.

**Conclusion.** Alongside its high view of the divinity of Jesus, the Fourth Gospel gives a clear picture of his humanity: his tiredness, thirst, tears, love, trouble, obedience and death. The statement is therefore true, and the two aspects are held together in the Gospel.
